paper_metadata.title: Relation Extraction with Matrix Factorization and Universal Schemas
paper_metadata.abstract: The paper proposes universal-schema relation extraction: a schema that unites textual surface-form predicates and relation types from existing structured databases. It populates this schema with matrix-factorization models that learn latent vectors for entity tuples and relations, enabling prediction of unobserved surface-pattern and database-relation facts. Jointly modeling New York Times textual relations and Freebase relations is reported to outperform state-of-the-art distant supervision.

problem_addressed: Relation extraction normally targets a fixed, finite schema and needs manually labeled text or an existing structured source with that schema. The paper seeks to populate a flexible universal schema, predict missing binary relation facts, generalize beyond explicit textual mentions, and jointly exploit textual surface patterns and Freebase relations.

methodology.description: The system constructs a sparse fact matrix whose rows are cross-document-resolved entity pairs and whose columns are both lexicalized dependency-path surface patterns and Freebase relations. It scores a relation–tuple cell with a logistic model. F factorizes relation and tuple embeddings; N sums directed relation-neighborhood weights for relations observed on the same tuple; E learns latent entity vectors and relation-slot vectors for selectional preferences. N, F, and E are combined additively (notably NFE). Training uses Bayesian Personalized Ranking over observed facts versus unobserved tuples, quadratic regularization, and stochastic gradient descent. In execution order: link NER mentions to Freebase entities using string matching; align entity pairs co-occurring in sentences; extract lexicalized dependency paths and retain patterns with at least 10 mentions; add training Freebase facts; train the ranking model; rank unobserved tuples separately for each target relation.

ontology_or_schema_use.value: Uses a universal schema rather than a fixed ontology: the union of relation schemas from structured sources such as Freebase and open-ended textual surface patterns. Freebase ontology types are deliberately not used as the entity model's predetermined types; the model instead learns latent entity representations. The authors propose future integration of universal entity types and attributes.

input_output.input_type: New York Times newswire text, Freebase facts, NER mentions linked to Freebase entities, and lexicalized dependency paths between co-sentential entity mentions.
input_output.input_granularity: A relation candidate is an ordered binary entity tuple aligned to a pair of entity mentions in the same sentence; each tuple aggregates its observed dependency-path patterns and, for training, its Freebase facts.
input_output.output_representation: Ranked, probabilistic binary relation instances: relation–entity-pair cells in a universal-schema matrix. Outputs include predicted Freebase facts and predicted textual surface-pattern relations.

datasets: New York Times Annotated Corpus: articles after 2000 for training and 1990–1999 for testing
Freebase facts and corresponding entity tuples, split 50/50 into training and test
Approximately 16,000 Freebase-related tuples after alignment/filtering (about 8,000 train and 8,000 test)
About 200,000 additional unrecorded-Freebase training tuples and 200,000 test tuples; evaluation uses a random 10,000-tuple test subsample

metrics: Average precision over each precision–recall curve
Weighted MAP, weighting each relation's average precision by its number of true facts
Sign test for per-relation statistical differences
baselines: MI09: distantly supervised classifier based on Mintz et al. (2009)
YA11: MI09 augmented with preprocessed pattern-cluster features from Yao et al. (2011)
SU12: Multi-Instance Multi-Label relation extractor from Surdeanu et al. (2012)
Ablations/comparators N, F, NF, and NFE
evaluation.setting: The authors train on observed NYT-pattern and Freebase facts, then evaluate two ranking tasks: prediction of Freebase relations and prediction of ten selected surface-pattern relations. For each relation as query, systems return their top 1,000 entity pairs; the top 100 answers from each system are pooled and manually judged. Results are restricted to a 10,000-tuple subsampled test set although models run on the complete data. Model settings are KF=KE=100 where applicable, 1,000 epochs, component regularization 0.01, and neighborhood-weight regularization 0.1.

value: On Freebase-relation prediction, Table 1 reports MAP / weighted MAP of 0.32 / 0.48 for MI09, 0.42 / 0.52 for YA11, 0.56 / 0.57 for SU12, 0.45 / 0.52 for N, 0.61 / 0.66 for F, 0.66 / 0.67 for NF, and 0.63 / 0.69 for NFE.
NFE has the best Freebase weighted MAP (0.69), whereas NF has the best MAP (0.66); NFE is significantly different by sign test from all compared systems except NF and F.
On ten surface-pattern relations, Table 2 reports MAP / weighted MAP of 0.22 / 0.28 for N, 0.44 / 0.56 for F, 0.44 / 0.50 for NF, and 0.43 / 0.46 for NFE.
The paper states the slowest proposed model trains in 45 minutes, versus four hours for YA11's topic model and two hours for SU12 on less data.

value: Author-stated: jointly modeling surface patterns and structured relations lets unstructured and structured data support one another and improves structured-relation prediction.
Author-stated: latent factorization can learn pattern–pattern correlations from unlabeled data and generalize to patterns unavailable in distant-supervision training.
Author-stated: learned latent entity representations capture selectional preferences without relying on predetermined entity types.
[Review inference] The explicit combination of text-derived and KB-derived columns makes this a direct graph-population and knowledge-fusion method, rather than only a fixed-schema text classifier.

value: Author-stated: the entity model harms weighted-MAP performance for surface-pattern relations; the paper attributes this to surface patterns admitting broader argument types than typed Freebase relations.
Author-stated: ranking evaluation is limited to a 10,000-tuple test subsample and a selected set of ten surface-pattern relations.

[Review inference] The pipeline depends on NER, simple string-match entity linking, and co-sentential entity-pair alignment; errors or ambiguity in these upstream steps can propagate to relation facts.

[Review inference] The method only treats binary relations in the presented experiments, although the paper says generalization to n-ary relations is possible; therefore n-ary performance is unverified here.

value: The authors note that Freebase's ontology types are often not sufficiently fine to discriminate relations, motivating latent entity representations instead of predetermined types.

The authors report that NFE can underperform on broad surface patterns because Freebase relations are typed while a pattern such as “X visits Y” permits several semantic types in each argument position.
The conclusion limits demonstrated scope to relation extraction and says universal-schema reasoning could additionally support data-integration tasks.
